periods.activity_title: From Raw Counts to Scaled Picture Charts

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the frequency table by counting children for each TV-watching duration from the notebook picture.
Answer 4 questions: how many watch more than half an hour, less than two hours, more than two hours; true/false comparison of two-hour vs half-hour watchers.
Suggest some ways for Joseph Uncle to show large numbers of items using pictures.
Choose your own scale and represent the same shop data using a pictograph in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the TV-watching scenario: children read the notebook picture and count how many friends fall into each duration category. The class completes Let us Do, p.180 ("Complete the frequency table by counting children for each TV-watching duration...."), working individually then sharing counts aloud to build a shared table on the board.

With the table on the board, children answer Let us Do Q1–Q4, p.180 ("Answer 4 questions: how many watch more than half an hour...."). Pairs discuss the true/false comparison before sharing answers; the teacher draws out how the organised table makes answering faster than re-counting the raw picture.

Pose the shop problem: Joseph Uncle has far too many items to draw one picture per item. Children respond to Let us Think, p.180 ("Suggest some ways for Joseph Uncle to show large numbers of items....") in a brief class discussion. The teacher introduces Dipesh's idea — one icon stands for 5 items — and displays the resulting pictograph, establishing the concept of scale.

Children choose their own scale (any sensible number) and create their own pictograph for the same shop data in their notebooks, tackling Let us Do, p.181 ("Choose your own scale and represent the same shop data...."). Volunteers share their scale choices and the class discusses why different scales produce different numbers of icons for the same data.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is forgetting to multiply the number of icons by the scale value when reading a pictograph — children often read icon count as the actual count. When the class discusses Joseph Uncle's pictograph, ask: 'If there are 4 toy icons and each stands for 5 toys, how many toys are there?' to surface and correct this early. The frequency table task (where categories include ½ hr and 1½ hr) is a good moment to check that children can read fractional hour labels without confusing them.

section_titles: Recording a Day — Pictograph vs Bar Graph
periods.activity_title: Reading Scaled Pictographs, Meeting the Bar Graph

tasks_in_class.description: Answer 4 questions from the two-wheelers pictograph: most two-wheelers day, total over three days, difference Monday vs Wednesday, difference Friday vs Wednesday.
Choose any other scale and represent the same two-wheeler data using a pictograph in your notebook.
Discuss in class: how is Sheela's recording (bar graph) different from Raman's recording (pictograph)?
Answer 5 questions comparing Raman's and Sheela's daily routines: sleeping, school hours, studying hours, same-time activities, whose routine is more balanced.

time_bands.activity: Children open to the two-wheelers pictograph (scale: 1 icon = 3 two-wheelers) and work through Let us Do Q1–Q4, p.182 ("Answer 4 questions from the two-wheelers pictograph: most two-wheelers day, total over three days...."). The teacher circulates, checking that children multiply correctly and record differences by subtraction.

Children select their own scale for the two-wheeler data and draw a fresh pictograph in their notebooks — Let us Do Q5, p.182 ("Choose any other scale and represent the same two-wheeler data...."). Two or three volunteers sketch their pictographs on the board; the class compares how a larger scale reduces the number of icons without changing the underlying counts.

Introduce Raman's pictograph and Sheela's bar graph side by side. Children discuss Let us Discuss, p.183 ("How is Sheela's recording different from Raman's recording?") in pairs first, then share with the class. The teacher lists key differences on the board: bars replace icons, axes are labelled, no scale factor needed to count.

Children answer Let us Do Q1–Q5, p.183 ("Answer 5 questions comparing Raman's and Sheela's daily routines...."). The teacher uses Q5 — whose routine is more balanced — to open a brief whole-class reflection on what balanced means and how graphs make such judgements visible.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who organised data into frequency tables and drew scaled pictographs often carry the scale-multiplication habit into bar graph reading — they may try to apply a scale factor to bar heights even when bars are drawn to a direct unit scale. Clarify that in Sheela's bar graph each unit on the vertical axis equals one hour directly. A frequent subtraction error is taking the smaller count from the larger on a different day and mis-labelling the answer; encourage children to write the day names alongside the numbers when finding differences.

periods.activity_title: My Own Bar Graph — Data from Life and Body

tasks_in_class.description: Record your own daily routine (24 hours) in hours and minutes for activities like sleeping, studying, playing, eating, and others in the table.
Make a bar graph of the time you spend on different activities using the grid provided.
Cut paper strips to the length of each friend's index finger and paste them along the horizontal line in the given bar graph.
Answer 4 questions from your paper-strip bar graph: whose finger is longest, length of longest, length of smallest, whose it belongs to.

time_bands.activity: Each child records their own 24-hour daily routine in the table provided — Let us Do, p.184 ("Record your own daily routine in hours and minutes for sleeping, studying, playing, eating, and others...."). The teacher reminds the class that all activity times must sum to 24 hours, supporting children who struggle to partition their day.

Using the same personal data, children construct their own bar graph on the grid provided — Let us Do, p.184 ("Make a bar graph of the time you spend on different activities...."). The teacher circulates, checking that bar heights correspond to the hours recorded and that axes are labelled with activity names and hours.

Children measure one another's index fingers with a ruler, cut paper strips to those exact lengths, and paste the strips as bars along the horizontal axis in their textbook — Let us Do, p.184–185 ("Cut paper strips to the length of each friend's index finger and paste them...."). The teacher emphasises that each strip's length directly encodes the measurement, making this a physical bar graph.

Children read their completed paper-strip bar graph and answer Let us Do Q1–Q4, p.185 ("Answer 4 questions from your paper-strip bar graph: whose finger is longest, length of longest...."). A quick show-of-hands confirms how many found the same person having the longest finger across the group.

periods.teacher_notes: When children record their daily routine, a common error is allocating hours that do not total 24; prompt children to add their column before drawing the graph. In the paper-strip activity, children sometimes paste strips without aligning the base to the horizontal axis, producing bars of different apparent heights despite identical lengths — check alignment before children answer comparison questions.
materials: Paper strips (pre-cut rolls or scrap paper)

section_titles: Food Wastage in the School Canteen
periods.activity_title: Reading Bar Graphs: Food Waste and Real Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Answer 6 questions from the food wastage bar graph: highest wastage item, least wastage item, total wastage, children that could be fed, comparison across days, predict next week's wastage.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the food wastage context: a bar graph shows how many kilograms of food Rani's school canteen wastes each weekday, with a different food item each day. The class reads the axes together — vertical axis in kilograms, horizontal axis listing the days — establishing what each bar represents before answering any questions.

Children work through Let us Do Q1–Q6, p.186 ("Answer 6 questions from the food wastage bar graph: highest wastage item, least wastage item, total wastage....") individually. Q4 requires a unit-rate calculation — 1 kg of wasted food could feed 3 children — so the teacher pauses the class briefly after Q3 to clarify: 'Multiply the total kg by 3 to find how many children could be fed.'

The class discusses answers as a group. The teacher records each answer on the board and asks children to explain their reasoning aloud, especially for Q5 (comparison across days) and Q6 (prediction for next week). Children who reached different answers for Q6 share their reasoning, opening a discussion about what a prediction means and what information supports it.

The teacher steers a brief value-based conversation: 'What could the school do to reduce food wastage?' Children offer suggestions freely. This connects the data to a real decision, reinforcing why reading and interpreting bar graphs matters beyond the mathematics classroom.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error in Q4 is dividing the total by 3 instead of multiplying — children read 'feeds 3 children per kg' and reach for division. Write the unit rate on the board as '1 kg → 3 children fed' and ask the class to reason from there. Q6 (predict next week's wastage) has no single correct answer; accept any prediction the child can justify from the graph, and use disagreements to discuss what makes a prediction reasonable.

periods.activity_title: Reading a Picture: Careful Counting and True or False

tasks_in_class.description: Observe the picture of children and determine True or False for 8 statements about glasses, caps, books, and backpacks worn/held by boys and girls.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.187 and spend time studying the picture of school children silently. The teacher then asks: 'How many attributes can you count from this picture?' Children name caps, glasses, books, backpacks; the teacher lists them on the board, setting up the categories that the True or False statements will test.

Children work through True or False, p.187 ("Observe the picture of children and determine True or False for 8 statements about glasses, caps, books, and backpacks....") individually, writing T or F for each statement. The teacher encourages children to count carefully and to mark what they have counted on scratch paper before committing to an answer.

The class reviews each statement together. For each one the teacher asks a child to give the answer and explain the count. Where children disagree, the class re-counts together from the picture, reinforcing the habit of verification — going back to the data rather than accepting a first impression.

The teacher closes with a reflection connecting all units of the chapter: the same information about a group of people can be recorded as a tally, a frequency table, a pictograph, or a bar graph — or read directly from a picture. Children name one thing each representation makes easier to see, consolidating the chapter's central idea about organising and reading data.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is counting only boys or only girls when a statement refers to all children, or vice versa. Before the review, ask: 'Does this statement say boys, girls, or all children?' to build the habit of reading quantifier words carefully. The closing reflection drawing on frequency tables, pictographs, and bar graphs helps children articulate the purpose of each representation.

items.prompt: A storekeeper has 20 notebooks, 35 pens, and 15 rulers in her shop. She wants to show this data as a pictograph. Choose a scale of your own and draw the pictograph. Write the scale you chose.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any sensible scale is acceptable (for example, 1 icon = 5 items). With scale 1 icon = 5: notebooks = 4 icons, pens = 7 icons, rulers = 3 icons. The child must state the scale clearly and draw the correct number of icons for each item.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each item count by the chosen scale value to find the number of icons to draw.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may try scale 1 icon = 1 item first, then discuss why a larger scale helps; confident students can repeat using a different scale and compare the two pictographs.

exercise.description: Choose your own scale and represent the same shop data using a pictograph in your notebook.

items.prompt: Meena counts cars passing her house: 18 on Monday, 12 on Tuesday, and 24 on Wednesday. Using a scale of 1 icon = 6 cars, draw a pictograph. How many icons will you draw for each day?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Monday: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 icons; Tuesday: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 icons; Wednesday: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 icons. The pictograph must show the correct number of icons for each day with the scale stated.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each day's count by the scale value (6) to find the number of icons.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first write the division sentence (18 ÷ 6 = ?) for each day before drawing; confident students can choose a different scale and redraw the pictograph.

exercise.description: Choose any other scale and represent the same two-wheeler data using a pictograph in your notebook.

items.prompt: Anil spends 8 hours sleeping, 6 hours at school, 2 hours studying, 3 hours playing, and 5 hours on other activities. Draw a bar graph to show this data. Label the horizontal axis with activity names and the vertical axis with hours.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Bar graph with five bars: Sleeping = 8 units tall, School = 6, Studying = 2, Playing = 3, Others = 5. Axes must be labelled. Total = 24 hours (correct partition of a day).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw each bar to a height matching the number of hours for that activity, reading directly from the data table.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first fill a two-column table (activity, hours) and then draw one bar at a time; confident students can add a second colour to show which activities together make exactly 12 hours.

exercise.description: Make a bar graph of the time you spend on different activities using the grid provided.

items.prompt: Four friends measure their index fingers: Priya 6 cm, Rohan 5 cm, Sana 7 cm, Dev 4 cm. They paste paper strips of these lengths as bars on a graph. Which of the following correctly describes the bar graph they will see?

options.label: A
options.text: Dev's bar is the tallest and Priya's bar is the shortest.

options.label: B
options.text: Priya's bar is the tallest and Dev's bar is the shortest.

options.label: C
options.text: Rohan's bar is the tallest and Sana's bar is the shortest.

options.label: D
options.text: Sana's bar is the tallest and Dev's bar is the shortest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sana's bar is the tallest (7 cm) and Dev's bar is the shortest (4 cm).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the four finger lengths directly: 7 > 6 > 5 > 4, so Sana has the longest and Dev the shortest.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have confused Priya (6 cm) with Sana (7 cm), perhaps misreading the largest value.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have reversed the comparison, picking the middle value as tallest and the actual tallest as shortest.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has inverted the comparison entirely, treating the smallest measurement as the tallest bar.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can write the four measurements in order from least to greatest before identifying tallest and shortest; confident students can state by how many centimetres the longest exceeds the shortest.

exercise.description: Cut paper strips to the length of each friend's index finger and paste them along the horizontal line in the given bar graph.

items.prompt: A frequency table shows: ½ hr — 8 children, 1 hr — 12 children, 1½ hr — 7 children, 2 hrs — 5 children, more than 2 hrs — 3 children. How many children watch TV for less than 2 hours?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Duration | Number of children |
| ½ hr | 8 |
| 1 hr | 12 |
| 1½ hr | 7 |
| 2 hrs | 5 |
| More than 2 hrs | 3 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 27 children. Add the counts for ½ hr, 1 hr, and 1½ hr: 8 + 12 + 7 = 27.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add only the categories strictly less than 2 hours: ½ hr, 1 hr, and 1½ hr.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child added all five categories (total of all 35 children), not reading 'less than 2 hours' carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child included the 2 hrs category (8 + 12 + 7 + 5 = 32), misreading 'less than 2' as 'up to and including 2'.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child added only ½ hr and 1½ hr, skipping the 1 hr category, suggesting a misread of the table.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can underline the phrase 'less than 2 hours' and tick only those rows before adding; confident students can also state how many children watch for 2 hours or more and verify that both groups sum to 35.

exercise.description: Answer 4 questions: how many watch more than half an hour, less than two hours, more than two hours; true/false comparison of two-hour vs half-hour watchers.

items.prompt: A pictograph uses 1 icon = 5 items. Toys show 6 icons, board games show 4 icons, and sports items show 3 icons. Explain in one sentence why drawing one picture for each item would not be practical, and then write how many play items (toys + sports items) the shop has in total.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One picture per item would not be practical because there are too many items to draw individually (e.g., 30 toys would need 30 drawings). Total play items: toys = 6 × 5 = 30, sports items = 3 × 5 = 15, total = 45 play items.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each icon count by the scale (5) to get the actual count, then add toys and sports items.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first complete the multiplication for each category separately before adding; confident students can suggest what scale they would choose if the shop had 200 of each item and explain why.

exercise.description: Suggest some ways for Joseph Uncle to show large numbers of items using pictures.

items.prompt: A pictograph shows two-wheelers passing a house using scale 1 icon = 3. Monday has 5 icons, Wednesday has 3 icons, Friday has 4 icons. How many more two-wheelers passed on Monday than on Wednesday?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each day's icon count by the scale (3) to find actual counts, then subtract Wednesday from Monday.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child subtracted icon counts directly (5 − 3 = 2) without applying the scale, forgetting to multiply.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child found Monday's total (15) but subtracted only Wednesday's icon count (3 icons, not 9 two-wheelers), mixing icons and actual values.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child found the icon difference (5 − 3 = 2) and multiplied by the scale incorrectly, or confused the scale with the answer.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can write the actual count next to each day's icon row before finding the difference; confident students can also find by how many two-wheelers Friday differs from Wednesday.

exercise.description: Answer 4 questions from the two-wheelers pictograph: most two-wheelers day, total over three days, difference Monday vs Wednesday, difference Friday vs Wednesday.

items.section_title: Recording a Day — Pictograph vs Bar Graph
items.prompt: Raman records his daily routine as a pictograph with 1 icon = 1 hour. Sheela records hers as a bar graph with the vertical axis showing hours. Name one way in which reading data is easier from Sheela's bar graph than from Raman's pictograph.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any valid difference is acceptable, for example: In Sheela's bar graph the height of the bar directly shows the number of hours by reading the axis, whereas in Raman's pictograph you must count individual icons. Alternatively: the bar graph does not need a scale multiplier since each unit on the axis equals one hour directly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare how the value is read: axis reading in a bar graph versus icon counting in a pictograph.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can look at both representations in their book and point to where they read the number before writing; confident students can name one situation where a pictograph might be preferred over a bar graph.

exercise.description: Answer 5 questions comparing Raman's and Sheela's daily routines: sleeping, school hours, studying hours, same-time activities, whose routine is more balanced.

items.prompt: Five students paste paper strips of their index finger lengths as bars: Anil 5 cm, Bina 8 cm, Chetan 6 cm, Diya 4 cm, Ela 7 cm. Which student's bar is the second longest?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ela (7 cm). Ordered from longest: Bina 8 cm, Ela 7 cm, Chetan 6 cm, Anil 5 cm, Diya 4 cm. The second longest is Ela.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Order all five lengths from greatest to least and identify the value in second position.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child identified the longest bar (Bina, 8 cm) rather than the second longest, not reading 'second' in the question.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have identified the middle value (6 cm, third position) rather than the second, or misranked the values.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have confused second longest with second shortest, or misread Anil's 5 cm as a higher value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can write all five measurements in order from largest to smallest and then point to the second entry; confident students can state by how many centimetres the second longest exceeds the second shortest.

exercise.description: Answer 4 questions from your paper-strip bar graph: whose finger is longest, length of longest, length of smallest, whose it belongs to.

items.section_title: Food Wastage in the School Canteen
items.prompt: A bar graph shows food wasted at a school canteen: Monday 4 kg, Tuesday 7 kg, Wednesday 2 kg, Thursday 5 kg, Friday 6 kg. If 1 kg of wasted food could have fed 3 children, how many children could have been fed with the total food wasted across the week?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Day | Food Wasted (kg) |
| Monday | 4 |
| Tuesday | 7 |
| Wednesday | 2 |
| Thursday | 5 |
| Friday | 6 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 72 children. Total wastage = 4 + 7 + 2 + 5 + 6 = 24 kg. Children fed = 24 × 3 = 72.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all five daily wastage values to find the total, then multiply by 3 (children fed per kg).

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child found the correct total (24 kg) but stopped there, not completing the multiplication by 3.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have divided 24 by 3 instead of multiplying, inverting the unit-rate relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have added only some days (e.g., 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 or similar partial sum) and then multiplied, or used a wrong total of 12 × 3.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first add the kg column and write the total, then write '? × 3 = total kg × 3' as a sentence before computing; confident students can calculate how many more children could be fed if wastage on Tuesday were reduced to 3 kg.

exercise.description: Answer 6 questions from the food wastage bar graph: highest wastage item, least wastage item, total wastage, children that could be fed, comparison across days, predict next week's wastage.

items.prompt: A picture shows 12 children in a classroom. 5 boys are wearing caps and 3 girls are wearing caps. The statement says: 'More than half the children are wearing caps.' Is this statement True or False?

options.label: A
options.text: False — only 8 out of 12 children are wearing caps, which is more than half.

options.label: B
options.text: False — only the boys are wearing caps, so it cannot be more than half.

options.label: C
options.text: True — 8 out of 12 children are wearing caps, which is more than half of 12.

options.label: D
options.text: True — all 12 children are wearing caps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: True. Total children wearing caps = 5 + 3 = 8. Half of 12 = 6. Since 8 > 6, more than half the children are wearing caps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add boys and girls wearing caps (5 + 3 = 8), compare with half of 12 (which is 6), and judge whether 8 exceeds 6.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child correctly counted 8 cap-wearers but then labelled the statement False, showing a comparison error — they did not check 8 against half of 12.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child considered only boys in the count, ignoring the girls who also wear caps, missing the instruction to count all children.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child assumed all children wear caps without counting, showing a lack of careful observation from the data.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first count cap-wearers and write 'half of 12 = ?' before comparing; confident students can write a new True or False statement of their own about a different attribute and challenge a partner.

exercise.description: Observe the picture of children and determine True or False for 8 statements about glasses, caps, books, and backpacks worn/held by boys and girls.

items.prompt: The table below shows how many children spend different amounts of time reading each day. How many children read for 1 hour or more each day?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Time spent reading | Number of children |
| ½ hr | 6 |
| 1 hr | 9 |
| 1½ hr | 5 |
| 2 hrs | 4 |
| More than 2 hrs | 2 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20 children. Add counts for 1 hr, 1½ hr, 2 hrs, and more than 2 hrs: 9 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify all rows where time is 1 hour or more and add their counts.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child added all five rows (total 26), not reading the condition '1 hour or more' and including the ½ hr row.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child added only the last three rows (1½ hr, 2 hrs, more than 2 hrs: 5 + 4 + 2 = 11 — see D — or a different partial sum), possibly misreading '1 hour or more' as 'more than 1 hour'.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child added only the 1½ hr and 2 hrs rows (5 + 4 + 2 = 11), omitting the 1 hr row, treating '1 hour or more' as 'more than 1 hour'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can underline '1 hour or more' and tick every row that qualifies before adding; confident students can write how many children read for less than 1 hour and verify both groups sum to 26.

exercise.description: Complete the frequency table by counting children for each TV-watching duration from the notebook picture.
